blocks.title: Retardation factor Rf
blocks.text: Each component has a specific retardation factor: Rf = (distance travelled by the component from the original spot) / (distance travelled by the solvent from the original spot).

In the chromatogram of Figure 15.10, sample A contains both components B and C, whose Rf values are Rf(B) = x/y and Rf(C) = x'/y. Paper chromatography is a convenient way of checking whether a substance formed in a reaction is pure or impure, using a suitable solvent in which it dissolves: a pure substance gives one spot, an impure substance more than one. A chromatogram also identifies substances by comparison with known pure samples; two substances are likely to be identical if they have the same Rf. In Figure 15.10 the impure substance shows two coloured spots, which have travelled the same distances as the reference pure compounds. The Rf value is always the same for a particular substance when the same stationary and mobile phases are used.

blocks.alt: Chromatogram of three samples A, B and C. A shows a black upper spot and a blue lower spot; B shows only the blue spot and C only the black spot. y is the distance from the base line to the solvent front; x and x' are the distances from the base line to the blue and black spots.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.10: Chromatogram (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.10).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 15.10 marks the spot distances only as '1' (one of them measured between the spots), and the text gives Rf(C) = x/y. Each distance is measured from the base line: x for B and x' for C, so Rf(B) = x/y and Rf(C) = x'/y, as drawn above.
